title: Breaking the Vault: Bypassing Chatbot Limits via Race Conditions & Response Manipulation
summary_en: An attacker bypassed a 5-conversation chatbot limit by using a race condition to generate extra session IDs and manipulating server responses to trick the frontend. This allowed for unlimited resource consumption and a potential Denial of Wallet attack against the provider's AI infrastructure.

lesson.cause: The vulnerability stems from a Time-of-Check to Time-of-Use (TOCTOU) flaw where the server checks the conversation count in the database without using atomic operations or locks. This allows multiple requests sent at the exact same millisecond to pass the check simultaneously. Additionally, the application relied on client-side state for UI enforcement and failed to re-verify session validity when the frontend was tricked into accepting a manually injected conversation ID.
lesson.walkthrough:
RECON
1. The researcher identified a business rule limiting users to 5 active chatbot conversations in the UI (User Interface: the buttons and menus you see on screen).
2. The researcher opened the browser's network tools to identify the endpoint (a specific web address that performs a task) responsible for starting new chats.
DISCOVERY
3. The researcher created 4 conversations to reach the threshold where the next request would be the limit.
4. The researcher prepared to send the 5th request while using Burp Suite (a tool used to catch and change web traffic between a browser and a server).
EXPLOITATION (PHASE 1: RACE CONDITION)
5. The researcher intercepted the request to initialize a new conversation.
POST /redacted/api/v1/chatbot/conversations/init HTTP/2
Host: redacted.com
{"platform":"website"}
Why: This HTTP request (a message sent from your computer to a server) tells the backend (the hidden part of the website that processes data) to start a new chat.
6. The researcher sent this request to Turbo Intruder, a tool designed to send many requests at the exact same time.
7. The researcher configured the tool to fire 5 identical requests simultaneously.
8. The researcher observed that the server returned multiple success messages instead of just one.
HTTP/2 200 OK
Why: 200 OK is a status code (a number from a server) meaning the request worked. The server checked the database (a digital filing cabinet) for all 5 requests before any of them finished updating the count.
9. The researcher saved one of the extra "conversation_id" values (a unique token identifying a chat) generated by these successful requests.
EXPLOITATION (PHASE 2: FRONTEND BYPASS)
10. The researcher refreshed the page and saw the "New Conversation" button was disabled because the UI correctly counted 5+ chats.
11. The researcher intercepted the request used to fetch the list of active chats.
GET /redacted/api/v1/chatbot/conversations HTTP/2
Why: This request asks the server for the data the browser uses to decide if the "New" button should be clickable.
12. The researcher viewed the server's response, which contained a JSON array (a list of data items) of the active chats.
13. The researcher deleted one chat object from the list in the intercepted response.
14. The researcher forwarded the modified response to the browser.
15. The researcher observed the "New Conversation" button was now enabled because the browser was tricked into thinking only 4 chats existed.
EXPLOITATION (PHASE 3: BACKEND BYPASS)
16. The researcher clicked the "New Conversation" button to trigger a fresh creation request.
17. The server correctly rejected the request because the database knew the real count was too high.
HTTP/2 429 Too Many Requests
Why: A 429 error is a status code meaning the user has exceeded a rate or quantity limit.
18. The researcher intercepted this 429 error response before the browser could process it.
19. The researcher changed the status code from "429" to "200 OK".
20. The researcher replaced the error message in the response body with a fake success message.
21. The researcher injected the "conversation_id" saved from Step 9 into this fake message.
{"status": "success", "conversation_id": "[RACE_CONDITION_ID]", "message": "User registered..."}
Why: This tricks the frontend into believing the server successfully created a new, valid chat session.
IMPACT
22. The researcher opened the new chat window and sent a message.
23. The researcher confirmed the backend processed the message using the injected ID, proving the limit was bypassed.
24. The researcher concluded this could lead to a Denial of Wallet (DoW) attack, where an attacker drains the company's money by forcing their AI to process thousands of unauthorized, expensive requests.
lesson.takeaway: When hunting for bugs, always look for features with strict numerical limits, such as 'Max 3 files,' 'One coupon per user,' or '5 free searches.' Use tools like Burp Suite's 'Send group in parallel' to test if the server can handle multiple requests at the exact same time without losing count. A common mistake is assuming that if the frontend (the browser) blocks an action, the backend (the server) is safe; always try to manipulate the server's responses to see if the frontend can be tricked into performing unauthorized actions. Variants of this bug include 'double-spending' in financial apps or 'double-voting' in polls.
lesson.fix: To fix this, the backend must use atomic database operations or row-level locking to ensure that the 'check' and 'update' steps happen as a single, unbreakable unit. Instead of checking the count and then updating it in two steps, use a single SQL query: 'UPDATE users SET chat_count = chat_count + 1 WHERE user_id = ? AND chat_count < 5;'. If the count is already 5, the database will update zero rows, and the application can safely return an error. Additionally, the backend should never trust a conversation ID provided by the client unless it has been strictly validated against the user's current session state.

title: Insufficient Session Expiration leads to Account Takeover via Password Change
summary_en: A session management flaw allowed an attacker to use an expired session token to change a user's password, leading to full account takeover. The platform failed to invalidate tokens upon logout and did not require the current password for security updates.

lesson.cause: The root cause is insufficient session expiration, where the server fails to invalidate (make unusable) a session token (a secret key identifying a user) after logout. This occurred on the presentation platform's profile and password change endpoints (specific web addresses for tasks). The backend code accepted the 'auth_token' parameter (a piece of data in a request) regardless of whether the user had officially logged out. Furthermore, the password change feature lacked a requirement for the 'old password' or 2FA (an extra security code). This allowed a 24-hour window for an attacker to reuse a captured token to gain full control.
lesson.walkthrough:
RECON
1. The researcher logged into the presentation platform and captured the session token (a secret key identifying the user).
auth_token=abk193
Why: To identify the parameter (a piece of data in a request) used for authentication (proving who you are).
2. The researcher navigated to the user profile page to test for access control (rules about who can see what).
GET /user/profile HTTP/1.1
Why: To find an endpoint (a specific URL for a task) where user data can be modified.
DISCOVERY
3. The researcher attempted to change the account name using a token from a different account.
auth_token=[attacker_token]
Why: To test if the system properly checks if the token belongs to the account being changed.
4. The researcher observed that the name change was successful, indicating an initial access control flaw.
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Why: This confirmed the server was not strictly validating the relationship between the token and the specific user data.
5. The researcher logged out of the account to end the session (a temporary connection).
GET /logout HTTP/1.1
Why: To trigger the invalidation (making a token unusable) process on the server side.
6. The researcher logged back in to generate a new, active session token.
auth_token=[new_token]
Why: To establish a baseline for what a 'valid' current token looks like.
7. The researcher attempted to use the old token to change the name again.
auth_token=abk193
Why: To see if the server still accepts the token after logout, which is a sign of insufficient session expiration.
8. The researcher confirmed the name changed successfully using the old token.
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Why: This proved the server does not delete or blacklist tokens from its database when a user logs out.
EXPLOITATION
9. The researcher navigated to the password change feature to increase the impact of the bug.
POST /change-password HTTP/1.1
Why: To target a high-impact feature that could lead to Account Takeover (gaining full control of an account).
10. The researcher entered a new password in the form fields provided by the platform.
new_password=attacker_pass&confirm_password=attacker_pass
Why: To prepare the payload (the actual data being sent) for the password change request.
11. The researcher captured the password change request and replaced the active token with the old victim token.
Cookie: auth_token=abk193
Why: To exploit the fact that the server still considers the old token valid for critical actions.
12. The researcher sent the modified request to the server.
POST /change-password HTTP/1.1
Why: To execute the final step of the exploit and change the victim's password.
IMPACT
13. The researcher observed that the server accepted the old token and updated the password.
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Why: This confirmed that the password change endpoint lacks security protections like requiring the 'old password'.
14. The researcher logged out and successfully logged back in using the victim's email and the new password.
Login: victim@example.com / attacker_pass
Why: To prove a permanent Account Takeover (ATO) was achieved.
15. The researcher noted that the token remained valid for over 24 hours.
Validity: > 24 hours
Why: To demonstrate the long window of opportunity an attacker has to use a stolen token.
16. The researcher concluded that even if a victim clicks 'Logout', an attacker with the token maintains access.
Impact: Critical
Why: Because the server-side session is never truly destroyed until a long timeout occurs.
lesson.example: Imagine a site target.example where you log in and get a cookie 'session_id=xyz'. When you click 'Logout', the site deletes the cookie from your browser, but the server still has 'xyz' marked as 'active' in its database. An attacker who stole 'xyz' earlier can send a request: 'POST /account/email-update HTTP/1.1' with 'Cookie: session_id=xyz' and 'new_email=hacker@evil.com'. Because the server doesn't check if the user actually logged out or ask for the current password, it changes the email. Now the attacker can use the 'Forgot Password' feature to send a reset link to hacker@evil.com and take over the account. This works because the server failed to 'invalidate' (kill) the session on its end.
lesson.takeaway: Always test if session tokens (secret keys for sessions) remain functional after a logout or a password change. Look for critical endpoints (specific URLs for tasks) like 'change email' or 'change password' that do not require the user to enter their current password. Use tools like Burp Suite to capture a token, log out, and then try to reuse that token in a 'Repeater' request. A common variant is 'Session Fixation', where an attacker forces a specific token on a victim. A beginner mistake is assuming that because a cookie is gone from the browser, it is also gone from the server's memory.
lesson.fix:
To fix this, the server must implement strict session management. First, when a user logs out, the server must invalidate the session token in its database so it can never be used again. Second, when a password is changed, the server should automatically kill all other active sessions for that user. Third, critical actions like changing a password must require the user to provide their 'current password' or a 2FA code. Finally, tokens should have a short expiration time.

title: Private Bug Bounty Experience— Tata Play Bug Bounty Program
summary_en: An unauthenticated Spring Boot Actuator interface was exposed on a Tata Play subdomain, revealing sensitive infrastructure details and management endpoints like /shutdown.

lesson.cause: The vulnerability was caused by a misconfiguration in the Spring Boot framework where management endpoints, designed for internal monitoring, were exposed to the public internet. By default, Spring Boot Actuator provides several 'endpoints' (specific web addresses used for monitoring) that can reveal system health, environment variables, or even allow remote application shutdown if not explicitly secured with authentication (a login process).
lesson.walkthrough:
RECON
1. The researcher performed reconnaissance (the process of gathering information about a target) on Tata Play's subdomains to find interesting web services.

DISCOVERY
2. The researcher identified a subdomain running a Java-based application and attempted to access the Actuator index (a directory of management tools).
3. The researcher sent a GET request (a standard message used by browsers to ask a server for a page) to the following endpoint:
GET /actuator HTTP/1.1
Why: This request asks the server to list all available management functions. (An endpoint is a specific URL path that performs a task).
4. The server responded with an HTTP 200 OK status ( a code meaning the request was successful) and a JSON body (a structured text format used for data exchange).
5. The JSON response contained a list of links, including sensitive ones like "shutdown" and "refresh".
6. The researcher then checked the health endpoint to see what information it revealed.
7. The researcher sent the following request:
GET /actuator/health HTTP/1.1
Why: This endpoint is used to check if the application is running, but it often leaks details about the underlying infrastructure like database status.
8. The server returned detailed information about the application's internal health and infrastructure components.

EXPLOITATION
9. The researcher noted the presence of the shutdown endpoint:
"shutdown": { "href": "https://[redacted]/actuator/shutdown", "templated": false }
Why: This indicates that the application might allow an unauthenticated user to stop the entire service. (Unauthenticated means the user has not logged in).
10. The researcher followed ethical guidelines and did not attempt to trigger the shutdown, as this would cause a Denial of Service (an attack that makes a service unavailable to users).
11. The researcher observed that while some endpoints returned an HTTP 403 Forbidden (a code meaning access is denied), the main index and health data remained public.

IMPACT
12. The researcher documented the findings, showing that an attacker could gain deep knowledge of the server's setup or potentially crash the application.
lesson.example:
Imagine a fictional company 'target.example' that uses Spring Boot for its backend. A researcher finds that the developers forgot to secure the management tools. 

1. The researcher visits: https://api.target.example/actuator/env
2. The server responds with a list of all environment variables (settings used by the app).
3. Inside the response, the researcher finds: "DB_PASSWORD": "SuperSecret123!"
4. This happens because the 'env' endpoint (which shows environment settings) was not restricted to administrators. 

An attacker could now use this password to log into the company's database and steal user data.
lesson.takeaway: When hunting for bugs, always check for common framework-specific paths like '/actuator', '/heapdump', or '/env' on Java applications. Use automated scanners or wordlists (lists of common file names) to find these hidden management interfaces. A key signal is finding a server that returns a JSON list of links when you visit '/actuator'. A common mistake is assuming that if the main '/actuator' page is blocked, the sub-pages are also blocked; always test individual endpoints like '/actuator/health' or '/actuator/info' separately.
lesson.fix:
To fix this, developers should use Spring Security to ensure that all actuator endpoints require a valid administrator login. Additionally, sensitive endpoints like 'shutdown' should be disabled entirely if not needed. In the 'application.properties' file, you can restrict exposure using the following configuration:

management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=health,info
management.endpoint.health.show-details=never
management.endpoint.shutdown.enabled=false

This configuration ensures only basic health and info are visible, details are hidden, and the shutdown command is completely turned off.

title: How I found BAC leads to De-escalate the Administrator privilege
summary_en: A low-privileged user can strip an administrator of their permissions by sending them a team invitation, which triggers a logic error that downgrades the admin's account to a 'pending' state.

lesson.cause: The application's invitation logic failed to verify if an email address was already associated with an active, high-privileged account before processing a new invite. When the 'Internal User' (attacker) sent an invitation to the 'Administrator' (victim) at victim@gmail.com, the system likely updated the existing user record's status to 'pending' or 'invited.' This design flaw allowed a subordinate to overwrite the state of a superior account, effectively performing an unauthorized privilege de-escalation.
lesson.walkthrough:
RECON
Step 1: Identify the hierarchy of roles within the organization-based application.
Code: Administrator (Full Control), Internal User (Limited), External User (N/A)
Why: To understand the target (Administrator) and the attacker's starting position (Internal User). A Role is a set of permissions assigned to a user.

DISCOVERY
Step 2: Locate the user invitation feature available to the 'Internal User' role.
Code: [Invitation Functionality]
Why: This is the target endpoint where the vulnerability resides. An Endpoint is a specific web address or 'door' on a server where a function lives.

EXPLOITATION
Step 3: Identify the email address of the target Administrator.
Code: victim@gmail.com
Why: The email serves as the unique identifier for the account the attacker wants to disrupt.

Step 4: Use the 'Internal User' account to send a new invitation to the Administrator's email address.
Code: attacker@gmail.com invites victim@gmail.com
Why: The researcher is testing if the system allows 're-inviting' an existing user. A Parameter is a piece of information, like an email, sent to the server to process.

IMPACT
Step 5: Log in as the Administrator to check the account status.
Code: [Administrator Dashboard]
Why: To see if the invitation affected the existing account. The UI (User Interface) is the visual part of the website you click and see.

Step 6: Observe that administrative control buttons have vanished from the Administrator's view.
Code: "The buttons of accepting and ignoring had disappeared"
Why: The system processed the invite and downgraded the Admin's active session to a restricted 'pending' state. This is Privilege De-escalation, a bug where a user's power is reduced by an unauthorized person.
lesson.takeaway: When hunting for logic bugs, always test how 'Invite' or 'Add User' features handle emails that are already registered in the system. Look for instances where a system 'updates' an existing record instead of 'rejecting' the duplicate input. A common signal is when an app allows you to 're-send' an invite to someone who is already a member. A variant of this bug involves 'Self-Registration' where signing up with an existing admin's email might trigger a password reset or account merge. Avoid the mistake of assuming that 'Invite' forms only create new records; they often interact with existing ones.

title: Discovering and Responsibly Disclosing a Path Traversal Vulnerability in a WordPress Plugin
summary_en: A path traversal vulnerability in the Easy Testimonial Slider and Form WordPress plugin allowed attackers to delete arbitrary files on the server by manipulating the CAPTCHA cleanup process.

lesson.cause: The vulnerability stems from a lack of input validation in the plugin's CAPTCHA file deletion routine. The application accepted a file path or filename from the user and passed it directly to a file deletion function without checking if the path pointed outside the intended temporary directory. This allowed the use of 'dot-dot-slash' (../) sequences to navigate the server's file system and target sensitive files.
lesson.walkthrough:
RECON
1. Identify a WordPress website using the 'Easy Testimonial Slider and Form' plugin (version < 1.0.32).
2. Locate a public-facing page that displays a testimonial submission form.
DISCOVERY
3. Observe that the form includes a CAPTCHA (a security test to distinguish humans from bots).
4. Note that the CAPTCHA generates a temporary image file on the server's disk.
5. Use a web proxy (a tool like Burp Suite that intercepts traffic between your browser and the server) to monitor requests when the form is submitted or refreshed.
6. Look for a specific HTTP request (a message sent from your browser to the server) that handles the cleanup of old CAPTCHA images.
EXPLOITATION
7. Identify the parameter (a specific piece of data in the request) that specifies which file should be deleted.
8. We assume the application uses a parameter like 'captcha_file' to identify the target for deletion.
9. Attempt to manipulate this parameter by adding path traversal sequences.
10. Use the sequence '../' which tells the operating system to move up one directory level.
11. Construct a payload (a malicious piece of data) designed to reach a critical file, such as the WordPress configuration file.
12. Example payload: '../../../../wp-config.php'
13. Send the modified request to the server.
14. The server receives the request and processes the deletion command.
IMPACT
15. Because the server does not validate the path, it follows the '../' instructions out of the CAPTCHA folder.
16. The server deletes 'wp-config.php', which contains the site's database credentials.
17. The website immediately goes offline or enters a setup state because it can no longer find its configuration, resulting in a Denial of Service (DoS).
lesson.example: Imagine a fictional site 'target.example' that has a profile picture feature. When you change your picture, it deletes the old one using this URL: https://target.example/edit-profile?delete_old=user123_old.jpg. The server-side code looks like this: unlink('/var/www/html/uploads/' . $_GET['delete_old']);. An attacker changes the request to: https://target.example/edit-profile?delete_old=../../index.php. The server combines the paths to get '/var/www/html/uploads/../../index.php', which resolves to '/var/www/html/index.php'. The server then deletes the main homepage file because it blindly trusted the 'delete_old' input.
lesson.takeaway: Always look for features that handle file management, such as image uploads, downloads, or 'cleanup' routines. If you see a filename in a URL or POST parameter, try adding '../' to see if you can access or affect files in other folders. A common signal is a parameter ending in a file extension like .jpg or .pdf. Avoid the mistake of assuming that 'hidden' cleanup processes are safe; if the browser sends the filename, the user can change it.

title: When a “Secret” S3 Link Isn’t So Secret: IDOR in a Whistleblowing System
summary_en: An unauthenticated attacker can download confidential whistleblower attachments by simply using the S3 URL returned after upload, due to an IDOR that relies on secret URLs instead of proper access control.

lesson.cause: The application stores uploaded files in an Amazon S3 bucket but does not enforce any bucket‑level or application‑level access control. The server returns the full S3 URL in the response field `attached_file_path`, assuming the URL itself is secret. Because the bucket is publicly readable, anyone who knows the URL can retrieve the object without authentication. No additional checks (e.g., signed URLs, token validation) are performed when the URL is accessed. This design flaw turns the URL into an insecure identifier, enabling an Insecure Direct Object Reference (IDOR).
lesson.walkthrough:
RECON
Step 1: Submit the whistleblowing form with a test file.
- Action: Fill out the form, attach `Hello world.pdf`, and click submit.
- Why: This creates a new object in the S3 bucket (HTTP request = a message from browser to server; file = binary data).

Step 2: Intercept the server response with a proxy (e.g., Burp Suite).
- Action: Capture the HTTP response that contains JSON.
- Why: A proxy lets us view raw traffic (HTTP = protocol; response = data server sends back).

Step 3: Locate the `attached_file_path` field in the JSON body.
- Action: Find a line like `"attached_file_path":"https://s3.amazonaws.com/whistlebucket/abc123.pdf"`.
- Why: This field holds the direct S3 URL (URL = address of a resource on the web).

EXPLOITATION
Step 4: Copy the full S3 URL.
- Action: Highlight and copy the value after `attached_file_path`.
- Why: The URL points to the exact object stored in S3.

Step 5: Issue a GET request to the copied URL.
- Action: `GET https://s3.amazonaws.com/whistlebucket/abc123.pdf HTTP/1.1`
- Why: GET = request to retrieve data; the bucket returns the PDF because it is publicly readable.

Step 6: Observe the PDF content returned byte‑for‑byte.
- Action: The response body contains the PDF file.
- Why: No authentication or 403 (Forbidden) is required, proving the IDOR.

IMPACT
Step 7: Repeat the GET request with any other `attached_file_path` values observed in logs or traffic.
- Action: Use other URLs discovered from different uploads.
- Why: All files are exposed, leaking confidential whistleblower evidence.
lesson.example:
**Fictional target:** https://target.example/upload
**Vulnerable code snippet (pseudo‑Python):**
```python
file_url = f"https://s3.amazonaws.com/secret-bucket/{file_name}"  # builds public URL
return jsonify({"attached_file_path": file_url})
```
**Attack request:**
```
GET https://s3.amazonaws.com/secret-bucket/confidential_report.pdf HTTP/1.1
Host: s3.amazonaws.com
```
**Why it works:** The server returns a plain public URL without signing it. Because the S3 bucket allows `s3:GetObject` for anyone, the attacker can download `confidential_report.pdf` simply by requesting the URL. No token, cookie, or header is needed (HTTP GET = retrieve; public bucket = no access control).
lesson.takeaway: When testing file‑upload features, always look for URLs returned to the client after upload; a plain S3 or CDN link is a red flag. Use tools like Burp Suite or browser dev tools to capture the response and copy the URL. Variants include signed‑URL bypass (if signatures are predictable) and misconfigured Azure Blob or Google Cloud Storage links. Beginners often assume that a long, random‑looking URL is safe—remember that security must be enforced on the server, not hidden in the URL.
lesson.fix:
Enforce bucket‑level access control so objects are not publicly readable. Generate time‑limited, signed URLs (e.g., AWS S3 pre‑signed URLs) when a user needs to download a file, and validate the request on the server side. Alternatively, store files in a private bucket and proxy downloads through an authenticated endpoint that checks the reporter’s permissions before streaming the file. Example fix (pseudo‑Python):
```python
# upload stores file in private bucket
s3.put_object(Bucket='whistlebucket', Key=file_name, Body=file_data, ACL='private')
# when download is requested, verify user and create signed URL
if user_can_view(report_id):
    url = s3.generate_presigned_url('get_object', Params={'Bucket':'whistlebucket','Key':file_name}, ExpiresIn=300)
    return jsonify({"download_url": url})
```
This removes the permanent public link and ensures only authorized users can retrieve the attachment.

title: Triaged to Spam: How Cosmos Dismissed Valid CosmWasm IBC v2 Bugs Before Shipping Patches
summary_en: Vulnerabilities in Cosmos CosmWasm allowed attackers to spoof source ports and authorize malicious packet acknowledgments by bypassing ownership checks in the IBC v2 implementation.

lesson.cause: The root cause was a failure to validate ownership of Inter-Blockchain Communication (IBC) ports—unique identifiers used to route messages between blockchains. In the vulnerable version of wasmd, the system checked if a port ID was provided but did not verify if the smart contract making the request actually owned that port. This allowed any contract to claim it was sending or acknowledging data on behalf of a different, legitimate contract.
lesson.walkthrough:
RECON
1. Identify the target as the Cosmos wasmd module, which allows WebAssembly (Wasm) smart contracts to interact with the Inter-Blockchain Communication (IBC) protocol.
2. Focus on the IBC v2 implementation (ibc-go v10) which handles how different blockchains send and confirm data packets.
DISCOVERY: ASYNC ACK AUTHORIZATION
3. Analyze the code in x/wasm/keeper/handler_plugin.go responsible for 'asynchronous acknowledgments' (a way for a contract to confirm it received a message later rather than immediately).
4. Observe the vulnerable logic in the IBC2RawPacketHandler function:
case msg.IBC2.WriteAcknowledgement != nil: if contractIBC2PortID == "" { ... }
5. Why: The code only checks if the contractIBC2PortID (the identifier for the contract's communication channel) is not empty. It does not check if the contract is the actual recipient of the packet it is trying to acknowledge.
EXPLOITATION: ASYNC ACK
6. A malicious contract identifies a pending packet intended for a victim contract.
7. The attacker calls WriteAcknowledgement using the victim's packet sequence and client ID.
8. Because the code lacks an ownership check, the system accepts the attacker's acknowledgment as valid, potentially triggering logic in the sender chain that should only happen if the victim responded.
DISCOVERY: SOURCE PORT SPOOFING
9. Analyze the message encoder in x/wasm/keeper/handler_plugin_encoders.go which prepares messages to be sent to other chains.
10. Observe how the SourcePort (the 'return address' of the message) is handled:
SourcePort: payload.SourcePort,
11. Why: The system takes the SourcePort directly from the contract's input without verifying if the contract owns that port. A 'Port' is like a specific phone extension on a blockchain's communication system.
EXPLOITATION: PORT SPOOFING
12. An attacker contract creates a SendPacket message but sets the SourcePort to the port ID of a high-value victim contract.
13. The system signs the message with the attacker's identity but keeps the victim's SourcePort in the payload.
14. The receiving chain and the original chain's callbacks (like 'on acknowledgment') treat the message as if it originated from the victim contract.
IMPACT
15. This allows an attacker to execute callbacks and state changes under the identity of any other contract on the chain, leading to potential fund theft or governance manipulation.
lesson.takeaway: When hunting for bugs in modular systems or cross-chain protocols, look for 'ID-only' validation. This occurs when a program checks if a parameter (like a Port ID or Account ID) is valid or non-empty, but fails to check if the current user has the authority to use that specific ID. Always look for functions that 'trust' a value provided in a message payload without cross-referencing it against a secure internal database or 'store'. A common signal is seeing a 'Signer' or 'Sender' field being correctly populated while the actual 'Source' or 'Owner' field in the data payload is user-controlled and unvalidated.

title: IDOR in a Third-Party AI Chat Widget: Sensitive Data Exposure
summary_en: An IDOR in a third-party AI chat widget allowed unauthorized access to user contact details, including phone numbers and internal tokens, by manipulating the email parameter in an API request.

lesson.cause: The vulnerability stems from an Insecure Direct Object Reference (IDOR) on a backend API endpoint used by a chat widget. An IDOR is a bug where an application provides direct access to data based on user input without checking permissions. The endpoint /backend/widget/contact/upsert used the email field as a lookup key to fetch existing records. Because the server did not verify if the requester was authorized to view the data linked to that email, it returned sensitive information to any user who knew a victim's email address.
lesson.walkthrough:
RECON
1. The researcher monitored the web platform's traffic using Burp Suite (a tool used to intercept and inspect web traffic).
2. They identified an AI chat widget making requests to a third-party domain instead of the main site's API.
DISCOVERY
3. To see how the widget handles data, the researcher updated their profile name.
4. They captured the following HTTP request (a message sent from a browser to a server):
POST /backend/widget/contact/upsert HTTP/2
Host: [redacted]
Content-Type: application/json
X-Bot-Token: [redacted]
{
 "name": "owners",
 "email": "my-email@example.com",
 "phone": "...",
 "customData": {
 "role": "Owner",
 "organizationToken": "org_...",
 "userToken": "user_..."
 }
}
Why: The POST method sends data to the server. The upsert endpoint (a combination of 'update' and 'insert') processes user details. The X-Bot-Token is a header (extra metadata) used for identification.
EXPLOITATION
5. The researcher suspected the server might return data based only on the email field.
6. They prepared a second account to act as the victim.
7. They sent a simplified request using the victim's email address:
POST /backend/widget/contact/upsert HTTP/2
Host: [redacted]
Content-Type: application/json
X-Bot-Token: [redacted]
{
 "email": "my-second-email@example.com"
}
Why: By removing other fields, the researcher tested if the server would treat this as a lookup request for the existing record tied to that email.
IMPACT
8. The server responded with the full contact record for the second account.
9. The response included the victim's name, phone number, role, and internal identifiers (userToken and organizationToken).
10. This confirmed that any user could retrieve another user's private data just by knowing their email address.
lesson.example:
Imagine a fictional site target.example.com that uses a support widget. When you open the chat, it sends your email to api.support-widget.com/v1/user/sync to load your history. An attacker sends a request like this:

POST /v1/user/sync HTTP/1.1
Host: api.support-widget.com
Content-Type: application/json
{
  "user_email": "victim@example.com"
}

The server sees "user_email": "victim@example.com" and, without checking if the requester is logged in as that user, returns the victim's phone number and home address in the response. This works because the server trusts the user_email parameter (a piece of data sent in the request) as the sole proof of identity.
lesson.takeaway: Always inspect third-party integrations like chat widgets, analytics, or support tools, as they often have weaker security than the main application. Look for 'upsert,' 'sync,' or 'profile' endpoints that take a simple identifier like an email or a numeric ID. A common signal is when an API returns a full object (all user details) after you send a small piece of information. A variant of this is 'Leaky APIs,' where an endpoint meant for internal use is accidentally exposed to the public. Avoid the mistake of assuming that third-party code is inherently secure.

title: Could This Have Been a €1,000 Bug? My First Accepted Bug Bounty Report
summary_en: A publicly accessible container repository was discovered that allowed unauthenticated access to internal metadata and container resources, potentially exposing proprietary information.

lesson.cause: The vulnerability was caused by a misconfiguration in the access control settings of a container repository. Access control refers to the security rules that decide who can see or use specific data. In this case, an endpoint (a specific web address where a service is accessed) that should have required authentication (the process of proving your identity with a password) was left open to the public. This allowed the researcher to view internal metadata (data that describes other data, such as version numbers or internal paths) without any credentials.
lesson.walkthrough:
RECON
1. The researcher performed manual reconnaissance, which is the process of searching for information about a target's digital assets.
2. During this search, they identified a URL associated with a container repository (a storage system for software packages).
3. They noted that the asset appeared to be an internal resource but was reachable from the public internet.
DISCOVERY
4. The researcher navigated to the repository URL in a web browser.
5. They observed that the page loaded content immediately without asking for a username or password.
6. To investigate further, they opened Burp Suite, which is a professional tool used to intercept and inspect web traffic.
7. They captured an HTTP request, which is a message sent from the browser to the server asking for data.
8. They examined the HTTP response, which is the data the server sends back to the browser.
9. They checked the headers (extra information sent with a request) to see if any session cookies (small pieces of data used to track a logged-in user) were being required.
10. They confirmed that no authentication headers were necessary to view the content.
EXPLOITATION
11. The researcher began browsing the accessible directories within the repository.
12. They accessed metadata files, which contained technical details about the container images.
13. They verified that they could see internal resource names and configuration details.
14. They documented the specific URLs that were accessible without a login.
IMPACT
15. The researcher assessed the potential impact, noting that an attacker could use this information to understand the company's internal software structure.
16. They compiled the evidence, including screenshots of the exposed data.
17. They submitted a report to the bug bounty program explaining how the lack of access control exposed internal information.
18. Initially, the report was marked 'Out of Scope' (not eligible for a reward), but the researcher remained professional.
19. The company later re-evaluated the report and confirmed it was a legitimate security issue.
20. The report was officially 'Accepted,' and the researcher was awarded a bonus for their finding.
lesson.example: Imagine a company uses a private Docker Registry at 'registry.target.example' to store their website's code. A researcher finds this URL and tries to access the catalog of images by typing 'https://registry.target.example/v2/_catalog' into their browser. If the server is correctly configured, it should return a '401 Unauthorized' error. However, if it is misconfigured, it might return a JSON list of all private software images, such as '{"repositories":["internal-api", "secret-database-connector"]}'. This allows the researcher to see exactly what software the company is running internally without ever logging in.
lesson.takeaway: When hunting for bugs, always check subdomains for internal tools like container registries, CI/CD pipelines (like Jenkins), or code repositories. Look for signs that you are seeing more than a guest should, such as lists of internal project names or version numbers. A key signal is when an API endpoint returns data without you providing an 'Authorization' header or a login cookie. A common variant of this bug is an exposed '.git' directory or an unprotected cloud storage bucket. Finally, if a report is rejected but you are sure the impact is real, wait for a re-review or politely provide more context on why the exposure is dangerous.
lesson.fix: To fix this, the organization must implement strict Identity and Access Management (IAM) policies that require authentication for every request to the repository. This can be done by configuring the web server or the repository software to check for a valid JSON Web Token (JWT) or session cookie before serving any data. Additionally, internal resources should be placed behind a VPN (Virtual Private Network) or a firewall so they are not reachable from the public internet at all. A sample configuration for a registry might look like: 'auth: token: realm: https://auth.example.com/token', which forces the user to prove their identity before access is granted.

title: How I Bypassed a Region-Locked Comment Feature on a Public Bug Bounty Program
summary_en: The app hides the comments UI for users in certain regions, but the GraphQL API still allows any logged‑in user to read and post comments, exposing a client‑side only access‑control flaw.

lesson.cause: The region restriction was implemented only in the frontend UI, which decides whether to show the comment button based on the user’s location. The backend GraphQL resolvers that serve the comment list and creation do not perform any region check, so they accept requests from any logged‑in user. Because the server never validates the caller’s region, the UI’s hide/show logic is the only gate. This design flaw means the security rule exists in code that runs on the client’s device, not on the server that enforces policy. Consequently, an attacker can bypass the restriction simply by calling the API directly.
lesson.walkthrough:
RECON
Step 1: Identify that the comments feature is missing in the UI when accessing the site from a blocked country. Why: The UI hides the button, indicating a possible client‑side check.

Step 2: Open a second browser with a VPN located in a supported country and verify that the comments UI appears. Why: Confirms the feature is region‑dependent.

DISCOVERY
Step 3: Capture the network traffic from the VPN browser while loading the comment list. Why: We need the exact request the app sends to the server.
Step 4: Record the GraphQL request used to read comments (verbatim):
POST /graphql HTTP/2
Host: api.example.com
Authorization: Bearer <AUTH_TOKEN>
Content-Type: application/json

{ "operationName": "GetVideoComments", "variables": { "videoId": "<VIDEO_ID>", "page": 1 }, "query": "query GetVideoComments($videoId: String!, $page: Int) { video(id: $videoId) { id title comments(first: 10, page: $page) { totalCount edges { node { id text createDate } } } } }" }
Why: This request asks the server for the first page of comments for a specific video; it includes an auth token proving the user is logged in.

Step 5: Capture the request used to post a comment from the VPN browser. Why: To see how the app creates a new comment.
Step 6: Record the GraphQL mutation (verbatim):
POST /graphql HTTP/2
Host: api.example.com
Authorization: Bearer <AUTH_TOKEN>
Content-Type: application/json

{ "operationName": "CreateComment", "variables": { "input": { "videoId": "<VIDEO_ID>", "text": "Hello world" } }, "query": "mutation CreateComment($input: CreateCommentInput!) { createComment(input: $input) { status comment { id text createDate } } }" }
Why: This mutation tells the server to store a new comment; the payload contains the video identifier and the comment text.

EXPLOITATION
Step 7: Switch to the non‑VPN browser (the blocked region) and replay the captured "read comments" request, keeping the same auth token. Why: The server does not check region, so it returns the comment list.
Step 8: Replay the captured "create comment" mutation from the blocked region. Why: The server accepts the mutation and creates the comment, proving write access.

IMPACT
Step 9: Verify that the comment appears when reading the list again. Why: Confirms that both read and write operations succeed despite the UI being hidden.
Step 10: Document the successful bypass with screenshots or API responses as proof for the bounty report. Why: Evidence is required for validation and payout.
lesson.example:
Assume a fictional video site at https://target.example. The frontend hides the comment box for users whose IP resolves to "CountryX". The backend GraphQL endpoint is https://api.target.example/graphql.

Vulnerable backend resolver (pseudo‑code):
function getComments(videoId) { return db.comments.where(vId == videoId); }
function addComment(input) { db.comments.insert({videoId: input.videoId, text: input.text, user: input.userId}); return {status:"ok"}; }

No region check is performed.

Attack request to read comments (run from a blocked IP):
POST https://api.target.example/graphql
Content-Type: application/json
Authorization: Bearer abc123

{ "operationName":"GetVideoComments", "variables":{"videoId":"vid123","page":1}, "query":"query GetVideoComments($videoId: String!, $page: Int){ video(id:$videoId){ comments(first:10,page:$page){ edges{ node{id text} } } } }" }
Why it works: The server trusts the auth token only; it never looks at the requester's country, so it returns the comment list.

Attack request to post a comment:
POST https://api.target.example/graphql
Content-Type: application/json
Authorization: Bearer abc123

{ "operationName":"CreateComment", "variables":{"input":{"videoId":"vid123","text":"test"}}, "query":"mutation CreateComment($input:CreateCommentInput!){ createComment(input:$input){ status } }" }
Why it works: Same reason – no region validation, so the comment is stored.

The attacker can now read and write comments from any region.
lesson.takeaway: When a feature disappears in the UI for a certain geography, assume the restriction might be client‑side only and test the underlying API directly. Look for GraphQL or REST endpoints that handle the same operation and replay them with a valid auth token. Tools like Burp Suite, OWASP ZAP, or browser devtools can capture the requests. Variants of this bug appear as missing server‑side checks for age, subscription level, or feature flags. Beginners often forget to include the Authorization header when replaying, causing false‑negative results; always copy the full request, not just the JSON body.

title: Bug Hunting on Android: Finding an Old Session Bug After Password Change
summary_en: An application fails to invalidate existing user sessions after a password change, allowing potentially compromised sessions to remain active.

lesson.cause: The application's session management logic does not link session validity to the password's state or a 'last password change' timestamp. When a password is updated, the server fails to revoke or delete active session tokens (cookies) stored in its database or cache. This means the unique ID used to identify the user (the session cookie) remains trusted by the server even though the credentials that generated it have changed.
lesson.walkthrough:
RECON
1. Identify a target website that has a bug bounty program.
2. Create a test account on the target website.

DISCOVERY
3. Open two different browsers (e.g., Chrome and Firefox) or use an Incognito window.
4. Log into the same account on both browsers simultaneously.
5. In Browser A (Chrome), navigate to the password change settings.

EXPLOITATION
6. Change the account password in Browser A.
7. Observe the successful password change confirmation.
8. Switch to Browser B (Firefox/Incognito) where the old session is still active.
9. Refresh the page or attempt to access a protected area (like the profile page).

IMPACT
10. Confirm that Browser B is still logged in despite the password change.
11. Realize that an attacker who stole the session cookie before the password change still has full access.
Why: The server failed to perform session invalidation (the process of making a digital ID card no longer work).
lesson.example: Imagine a site target.example. A user logs in and gets a cookie 'session_id=abc123'. They change their password via a request to /update-password. If the server only updates the database password field but doesn't clear the sessions table, the 'abc123' cookie remains valid. An attacker with that cookie can still access /dashboard without knowing the new password.
lesson.takeaway: Look for this bug whenever an application handles sensitive account changes like password resets, email updates, or enabling Two-Factor Authentication (2FA). If the app doesn't 'log out all other devices,' it is a vulnerability. Use tools like Burp Suite to track session cookies across these actions. A common mistake is assuming that changing a password automatically clears all sessions; developers must explicitly code this behavior.

title: I Analyzed 12 IDOR-to-ATO Reports. The Email-Change Endpoint Wins.
summary_en: An insecure email‑change endpoint lets an attacker supply a victim ID and a trusted parameter to overwrite the victim’s email address (or add a secondary user / retrieve an API token), enabling full account takeover without any victim interaction.

lesson.cause: The root cause is an IDOR (Insecure Direct Object Reference) on the email‑change endpoint. The endpoint trusts a user‑supplied identifier (e.g., user_id) to locate the account but does not verify that the caller owns that identifier. Because the email field is treated as a trusted parameter, the server writes the supplied value directly to the victim’s record. The same flaw is reused for adding secondary users and for fetching API tokens, meaning the endpoint performs write operations without proper authorization checks. No additional factors such as CSRF tokens or captcha are required, so any authenticated attacker can exploit the flaw.
lesson.walkthrough:
RECON
Step 1: Identify the email‑change endpoint by browsing the web application or reading API documentation.
Payload: (no explicit payload shown)
Why: An HTTP request is a message sent from a client to a server; the endpoint URL is the address the request targets.

Step 2: Observe that the request includes a parameter that specifies the target user (e.g., user_id=123).
Payload: (no explicit payload shown)
Why: A parameter is a piece of data sent in the request URL or body; here it tells the server which account to modify.

EXPLOITATION
Step 3: Send a crafted request that sets user_id to the victim’s identifier and the email parameter to an attacker‑controlled address.
Payload: POST /api/v1/change_email HTTP/1.1\nHost: vulnerable.app\nContent-Type: application/json\n\n{"user_id": "456", "email": "attacker@example.com"}
Why: The JSON body is the payload; "user_id" tells the server which account, "email" is the new value. Because the server does not check ownership, it writes the attacker’s email to the victim’s record.

Step 4: Verify that the victim’s email has been changed by attempting a login or by checking the account profile.
Payload: (no explicit payload shown)
Why: Confirmation step ensures the write succeeded.

Step 5: Use the password‑reset flow (which sends a reset link to the newly set email) to set a new password and complete takeover.
Payload: POST /api/v1/password_reset HTTP/1.1\nHost: vulnerable.app\nContent-Type: application/json\n\n{"email": "attacker@example.com"}
Why: The reset endpoint trusts the email field; the attacker now receives the reset link.

ALTERNATE VECTORS
Step 6: Instead of changing email, add the attacker as a secondary user by supplying a secondary_user_id parameter.
Payload: POST /api/v1/add_secondary HTTP/1.1\nHost: vulnerable.app\nContent-Type: application/json\n\n{"user_id": "456", "secondary_user_id": "999"}
Why: The server writes the secondary user relationship without ownership checks.

Step 7: Or retrieve an API token for the victim by calling the token‑issue endpoint with the victim’s ID.
Payload: POST /api/v1/issue_token HTTP/1.1\nHost: vulnerable.app\nContent-Type: application/json\n\n{"user_id": "456"}
Why: The token endpoint returns a token that authenticates as the victim because it trusts the supplied ID.

POST‑EXPLOIT
Step 8: Use the stolen token or secondary account to perform any privileged action as the victim.
Payload: (no explicit payload shown)
Why: The token or secondary account acts as the victim’s credentials, granting full access.
lesson.example:
**Vulnerable snippet (fictional target)**
```python
# Flask endpoint that changes a user's email
@app.route('/change_email', methods=['POST'])
def change_email():
    data = request.get_json()
    uid = data['user_id']          # <-- attacker‑controlled identifier
    new_email = data['email']      # <-- trusted parameter
    user = db.get_user(uid)        # No check that uid belongs to the caller
    user.email = new_email        # Direct write without authorization
    db.save(user)
    return {'status':'ok'}
```
**Attack request**
```
POST /change_email HTTP/1.1
Host: target.example
Content-Type: application/json

{"user_id":"42","email":"attacker@evil.com"}
```
**Why it works**: The server trusts the `user_id` value and writes the supplied `email` directly to that record. Because there is no check that the caller owns `user_id`, the attacker can overwrite any user’s email, then use the password‑reset flow to take over the account. Each term (HTTP request, JSON, parameter, payload) is defined in the walkthrough above.
lesson.takeaway: When hunting for IDOR‑to‑ATO bugs, look for write‑oriented endpoints (email change, profile update, token issuance) that accept a user identifier as a parameter. Tools like Burp Suite or OWASP ZAP can help enumerate hidden parameters and test different IDs. Variants include changing phone numbers, security questions, or adding OAuth clients – any operation that writes identity data without proper ownership checks can lead to takeover. A common beginner mistake is to assume that authentication alone protects such endpoints; always verify that the server enforces that the caller’s identity matches the target identifier.
lesson.fix:
Add an explicit authorization check that the authenticated session’s user ID matches the `user_id` parameter before performing any write. For example, in the Flask snippet above:
```python
def change_email():
    data = request.get_json()
    uid = data['user_id']
    if uid != session['user_id']:
        return {'error':'unauthorized'}, 403
    new_email = data['email']
    user = db.get_user(uid)
    user.email = new_email
    db.save(user)
    return {'status':'ok'}
```
Return HTTP 403 Forbidden when the IDs differ. Apply the same pattern to secondary‑user addition and token‑issue endpoints. Additionally, consider using opaque references (e.g., UUIDs) and server‑side lookups based on the session rather than trusting client‑supplied IDs.

title: One Pending Invitation Was Enough to Restore Revoked Admin Privileges
summary_en: A flaw in the invitation system allowed a revoked administrator to regain control because pending invitations remained valid and retained their original permission levels even after the inviter was downgraded.

lesson.cause: The application's authorization logic (the system that checks if you are allowed to do something) only verified the inviter's permissions at the moment the invitation was created. It failed to perform a second check when the invitation was actually accepted. This created a 'time-of-check to time-of-use' flaw where a pending action (the invite) remained authorized even after the person who authorized it lost their own power.
lesson.walkthrough:
RECON
1. Identify the user roles in the application: Owner (full control), Administrator (can invite others), and Member (limited access).
2. Locate the invitation endpoint (the specific web address used to send invites) and the acceptance flow.

DISCOVERY
3. Log in to the application using an account with 'Administrator' privileges.
4. Send an invitation to a second email address you control, assigning it the 'Admin' role.
POST /api/team/invite
{"email": "attacker-alt@target.example", "role": "admin"}
Why: This creates a pending invitation in the database. An 'HTTP request' is a message your browser sends to a server to perform an action.

EXPLOITATION
5. Do NOT accept the invitation yet; leave it in a 'pending' state.
6. Log in as the 'Team Owner' (the highest authority).
7. Revoke the first account's privileges by downgrading it from 'Administrator' to 'Member'.
POST /api/team/update-role
{"user_id": "admin_a_id", "new_role": "member"}
Why: Now, the original inviter no longer has the 'privilege' (permission) to create admins.
8. Switch to the second email account (the one that received the invite).
9. Click the link in the invitation email to accept the invite.
GET /api/accept-invite?token=xyz123
Why: This triggers the application to process the invitation. A 'token' is a unique secret code used to identify a specific request.

IMPACT
10. Observe that the second account is successfully joined to the team with 'Admin' privileges.
11. Verify that this new Admin can now manage other users, effectively bypassing the Owner's decision to revoke the original Admin's power.
12. Confirm the new Admin can even downgrade the original Admin or the Owner, demonstrating full 'privilege escalation' (gaining higher permissions than intended).
lesson.example:
Imagine a fictional site 'target.example' that manages office access. 
1. Manager Alice creates a digital 'Guest Key' for Bob that grants 'Master Access'. 
2. Before Bob uses the key, the CEO fires Alice and deactivates her badge. 
3. Bob arrives and swipes his 'Guest Key'. 
4. The system checks the key and sees it was signed by Alice (who was a Manager at the time) and lets Bob in with Master Access, even though Alice is no longer authorized to grant that access. 

Attack Request:
POST /api/v1/invites/confirm
Host: target.example
Content-Type: json
{"token": "valid_token_from_revoked_user"}

title: Invalid Role Leads to Organization Lockout and Unauthorized API Access
summary_en: A role validation flaw allowed attackers to set an invalid role ID, resulting in a 'null' role state that bypassed API security checks and locked administrators out of managing the account.

lesson.cause: The backend application failed to verify if the role ID provided in the API request existed in the system's allowed list. When the researcher sent an unsupported value to the '/api/teams/<team_id>/users/<user_id>/roles/default' endpoint, the server accepted it without validation. This created a database entry with a 'null' role, which the application's logic was not designed to handle, leading to broken management features and inconsistent security enforcement.
lesson.walkthrough:
RECON
1. Identify the feature where administrators change user permissions and intercept the traffic using Burp Suite (a tool used to capture and modify data sent between a browser and a server).
DISCOVERY
2. Observe the standard request used to update a user's role.
PUT /api/teams/123/users/456/roles/default
Why: This is an HTTP request (a message sent to a server) using the PUT method (a command used to update existing data) to target a specific user's role settings.
3. Analyze the data sent in the request body.
{"userId": "<target_user_id>", "role": "1"}
Why: The body contains a parameter (a specific piece of information) named 'role' which uses a number to represent a permission level like 'Admin' or 'Developer'.
EXPLOITATION
4. Modify the 'role' value to an arbitrary, unsupported number.
{"userId": "<target_user_id>", "role": "5"}
Why: The researcher is testing if the server checks if '5' is a valid role before saving it to the database.
5. Send the modified request and observe the server's response.
HTTP/2 204 No Content
Why: A 204 response means the server successfully processed the request but has no data to return, indicating the invalid role was accepted.
IMPACT
6. Refresh the administrator's view of the user list.
The user's role now appears as 'null' (a term meaning 'no value' or 'empty').
7. Attempt to delete or edit the user with the 'null' role.
The interface fails to perform these actions.
Why: The management code likely expects a valid role string; when it sees 'null', the logic breaks, effectively locking the user into the organization.
8. Log in as the affected user and attempt to access restricted data.
GET /api/teams/123/users/info
Why: The researcher is testing API authorization (the process of checking if a user has permission to see data). Because the user has no valid role, the security check fails to find a 'restrict' rule and incorrectly allows access.
lesson.example: Imagine a website 'target.example' where users are '1' (Basic) or '2' (Pro). The update code looks like this: function setRole(id, val) { database.exec('UPDATE users SET role_id = ' + val + ' WHERE id = ' + id); }. An attacker sends a request with 'role=999'. The database saves '999'. Later, the site checks permissions: 'if (user.role == 1) { hide_pro_features(); }'. lesson.takeaway: Always test what happens when you send data that isn't in the official list, such as negative numbers, very large numbers, or symbols. A common variant is 'Type Juggling,' where sending a boolean 'true' instead of a number might bypass checks. Avoid the mistake of trusting that the frontend's dropdown menu is the only way a user can send a role ID.

title: My Bug Bounty Report Was Marked N/A. Then I Received $1,200.
summary_en: A researcher discovered an exposed API schema that revealed internal administrative endpoints, one of which allowed a low-privilege user to perform unauthorized administrative actions.

lesson.cause: The vulnerability was caused by two distinct failures: first, the API documentation (Swagger/OpenAPI schema) was publicly accessible without authentication, providing a map of internal functions. Second, the backend server failed to perform authorization checks on specific administrative endpoints, relying on 'security by obscurity' (assuming users wouldn't find the URL) rather than verifying the user's permissions.
lesson.walkthrough:
RECON
1. The researcher performed reconnaissance (the process of gathering information about a target) to find hidden files.
2. They identified an unauthenticated API schema endpoint, which is a blueprint file describing how the application's backend works.
GET /api/v2/swagger_doc HTTP/1.1
Host: api.example.com
Why: This request asks the server for its internal documentation. Because it didn't require a login, the server returned a full list of every available command (endpoint).

DISCOVERY
3. The researcher analyzed the documentation to find 'administrative operations' (actions only bosses or IT staff should do).
4. They found a specific route intended for administrators that was not visible in the normal user interface.
5. They logged into the application with a 'low-privilege account' (a standard user with no special powers).

EXPLOITATION
6. The researcher attempted to trigger the administrative action by sending a direct request to the discovered endpoint using their standard user credentials.
POST /api/admin/internal_operation HTTP/1.1
Host: api.example.com
Cookie: session=low_privilege_user_cookie
Content-Type: json
{"action": "modify"}
Why: This 'payload' (the data sent to the server) tries to perform an admin task. The researcher included their own session cookie (a digital ID card) to prove they were acting as a regular user.
7. The server responded with a success message instead of a '403 Forbidden' error.
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
{"success":true}
Why: The '200 OK' status code indicates the server accepted the command. This proves 'Broken Access Control' (when a system fails to stop a user from doing things they shouldn't).

IMPACT
8. To confirm this was a bug, the researcher tried other admin endpoints which correctly returned '403 Forbidden', proving the specific endpoint was uniquely vulnerable.
9. The researcher reported the 'Information Disclosure' (the leaked map) and the 'Unauthorized Access' (the ability to act as an admin).
lesson.example:
Imagine a website 'target.example' that has a hidden map of its office at 'target.example/building-plans.json'. A visitor finds this map and sees a button labeled 'Unlock Server Room' located at 'target.example/api/unlock'. Even though the visitor is just a guest, they send a digital request to that address. Because the door's computer only checks if the request is formatted correctly, but doesn't check if the person sending it is a Security Guard, the door unlocks. 

Request:
POST /api/unlock HTTP/1.1
Host: target.example
Cookie: user_type=guest

Response:
200 OK
{"status": "door_unlocked"}
lesson.takeaway: Always look for API documentation files like 'swagger.json', 'api-docs', or 'v2/swagger'. These files are 'treasure maps' that reveal hidden functionality. When you find an interesting endpoint, always test it with the lowest possible user permissions to see if the server actually checks 'Authorization' (permissions) rather than just 'Authentication' (identity). A common mistake is assuming that because a URL is 'hidden' or 'internal', it is safe from discovery.

title: IDOR + RBAC Vulnerability: Finding the Attack Scenario That Earned Me $100
summary_en: A Viewer role can delete admin‑only resources by sending a DELETE request to /example/{example_id} after enumerating IDs via an unauthenticated GET endpoint, resulting in an IDOR and broken access‑control bug.

lesson.cause: The DELETE /example/v1/example/example/{example_id} endpoint does not verify that the caller has admin privileges, only checking the Viewer role. The Viewer role is allowed to call the endpoint, so it can delete any object if it knows the ID. The GET /example/v1/Example/ID endpoint returns a list of all example IDs without any authentication or authorization checks, exposing the identifiers. Because IDs are discoverable, an attacker can combine the two endpoints to perform an IDOR (Insecure Direct Object Reference) and bypass role‑based access control.
lesson.walkthrough:
RECON
Step 1: Look at the API documentation or traffic and notice a DELETE endpoint.
GET https://example.com/example/v1/example/example/{example_id}
Why: This is an HTTP request (a message sent from client to server) using the DELETE method (asks server to remove a resource) with a path parameter {example_id} that specifies which object to delete.

Step 2: Test the endpoint with a known ID while logged in as a Viewer role.
DELETE https://example.com/example/v1/example/example/12345
Why: The server responded with success, showing the Viewer role is allowed to call the endpoint.

DISCOVERY
Step 3: Search for other endpoints that might reveal IDs.
GET https://example.com/example/v1/Example/ID
Why: This is an HTTP GET request (asks server to return data) that returns a list of all example IDs.

Step 4: Send the GET request without any authentication.
GET https://example.com/example/v1/Example/ID
Why: The response contains IDs like ["111","222","333"], proving the endpoint is publicly accessible.

EXPLOITATION
Step 5: Choose an ID that belongs to an admin‑only object (e.g., 222).
Why: Because the DELETE endpoint does not check ownership, any valid ID can be used.

Step 6: Send a DELETE request with the chosen ID.
DELETE https://example.com/example/v1/example/example/222
Why: The server deletes the admin resource, confirming an IDOR and RBAC bypass.

IMPACT
Step 7: Verify the resource is gone by re‑fetching the list or checking the UI.
GET https://example.com/example/v1/Example/ID
Why: The missing ID shows the deletion succeeded, demonstrating the impact of the bug.
lesson.takeaway: When hunting for IDOR + RBAC issues, look for endpoints that perform destructive actions (POST, PUT, DELETE) and compare them with any enumeration endpoints that return object identifiers without proper auth. Tools like Burp Suite or OWASP ZAP can help capture traffic and spot missing authorization checks. Variants include IDOR on update (PUT) or view (GET) endpoints and broken object‑level permissions in GraphQL mutations. A common beginner mistake is to assume that a role restriction on one endpoint protects the whole API; always verify each endpoint’s own access control.

title: Exposed Source Code Archive (ekinerja.zip) di Portal Pemerintah Kabupaten [REDACTED]: Kebocoran .env dan Hash Password Database
summary_en: A publicly accessible ZIP archive on a government portal exposed the entire application source code, database credentials, and user password hashes.

lesson.cause: The developer left a backup archive named 'ekinerja.zip' in the web root, which is the main folder where public website files are stored. This occurred because the web server was not configured to block access to sensitive file types like .zip or .env. The archive contained the application's secret configuration file and a full export of the database, which should never be accessible to the public.
lesson.walkthrough:
RECON
1. The researcher identified the target government portal for security testing.
2. The researcher performed directory fuzzing, which means using a tool to automatically guess many different file names to find hidden ones.
3. The researcher discovered a potential file named 'ekinerja.zip' in the main directory.
4. The researcher sent an HTTP request, which is a message sent by your browser to a server asking for a file.
https://ekinerja.redactedkab.go.id/ekinerja.zip
Why: To see if the server would allow a public user to download this specific resource (a file or page).
DISCOVERY
5. The server responded with the file, and the browser automatically began the download.
6. The researcher saved the 'ekinerja.zip' archive to their local computer.
7. The researcher used an extraction tool to unzip the contents of the archive.
8. The researcher noticed a file named '.env' in the root of the extracted folder.
EXPLOITATION
9. The researcher opened the '.env' file using a standard text editor.
.env
Why: A .env file is a text file used to store secret settings like passwords and system keys.
10. The researcher identified the 'APP_KEY' variable within the file.
APP_KEY=base64:...
Why: The APP_KEY is an encryption key, which is a secret code used to lock and unlock data like user sessions.
11. The researcher located the database username.
DB_USERNAME=ekinerja
Why: This is part of the credentials, which is the login information used to access the database (the system that stores all the site's data).
12. The researcher located the database password.
DB_PASSWORD=[REDACTED]
Why: This secret password allows anyone to connect to the database and read or change information.
13. The researcher explored the 'database/' folder within the extracted files.
14. The researcher found a file named 'kinerja.sql'.
kinerja.sql
Why: This is a database dump, which is a file containing a complete copy of all the information stored in the database.
15. The researcher opened the SQL file to inspect the data structure.
16. The researcher searched for the 'users' table within the file to find account information.
17. The researcher found the 'INSERT INTO' statements for user accounts.
INSERT INTO users (id, name, password) VALUES (1, 'admin', '$2y$10$...')
Why: This is an SQL query, which is a command used to talk to a database, and it reveals password hashes (scrambled versions of passwords).
IMPACT
18. The researcher confirmed that the 'admin' account hash was present and could be targeted.
19. The researcher noted that bcrypt was used for hashing, which is a specific method of scrambling passwords.
20. The researcher concluded that the database could be accessed remotely using the leaked credentials.
21. The researcher realized that user sessions could be hijacked using the leaked APP_KEY.
22. The researcher verified that the password hashes could be cracked offline to reveal the original passwords.
lesson.example: Imagine a fictional website at target.example. The developer creates a backup of the site before an update and names it 'backup_site.zip'. They leave this file in the main folder of the website. An attacker guesses the name and visits 'https://target.example/backup_site.zip'. After downloading and opening it, they find a file called 'config.php' containing the line: define('DB_PASSWORD', 'MySecretPass123');. Because the developer forgot to delete the temporary backup file, the attacker now has the password to the site's entire database.
lesson.takeaway: Always hunt for common backup patterns like [project-name].zip, backup.sql, or .env files during the recon phase. Use wordlists that include the target's name or common framework files to find these 'forgotten' archives. A key signal is finding a '200 OK' response for files that should normally be private or restricted. A common variant of this bug is the '.git' folder exposure, where the entire version history of the code is left online. Avoid the mistake of assuming 'hidden' files are safe just because there is no link to them on the homepage.

title: **Is Your Web App Leaking Files? How I Found a Path Traversal Vulnerability Leading to Local File Disclosure |**by [Samadhan Shimple](https://radiohackers.com/)
summary_en: A path traversal vulnerability was discovered in a file download endpoint, allowing an attacker to read sensitive system files like /etc/passwd by using directory navigation sequences.

lesson.cause: The application failed to validate or sanitize the 'file' parameter used in its download endpoint. It directly concatenated user input with a directory path on the server's filesystem without checking for directory traversal sequences like '../'. This allowed the input to 'escape' the intended folder and access the root directory of the operating system.
lesson.walkthrough:
PHASE: DISCOVERY
1. The researcher browsed the target application and identified a feature that allowed users to download or view files.
2. They used Burp Suite (a tool that intercepts and views web traffic) to capture the HTTP request (a digital message sent from a browser to a server).
3. They identified the specific endpoint (a web address that performs a task) and the parameter (a label for data) responsible for file selection.
GET /download?file=report.pdf HTTP/1.1
Why: The 'file' parameter tells the server which specific document to retrieve from its storage.
PHASE: EXPLOITATION
4. The researcher replaced the legitimate filename with a path traversal payload (a malicious input designed to trigger a bug).
GET /download?file=../../../../etc/passwd HTTP/1.1
Why: The '../' sequence tells the server's operating system to 'go up one folder level.' By repeating this, the researcher navigates from the web folder all the way to the system's root folder.
5. The researcher sent the modified request to the server to see how it would respond.
6. The server processed the request and, because it lacked security checks, followed the path provided in the payload.
PHASE: IMPACT
7. The server returned an HTTP 200 OK status ( a code meaning the request was successful).
8. The researcher examined the response body (the actual data sent back from the server).
9. The response contained the contents of the /etc/passwd file (a standard Linux file that lists all user accounts on the system).
10. The researcher observed the 'Content-Disposition' header, which confirmed the server was serving the system file as a download named 'passwd'.
attachment; filename=passwd
Why: This header tells the browser to treat the incoming data as a file download rather than a webpage.
lesson.example: Suppose a fictional website 'target.example' allows users to view their profile pictures via a URL like: https://target.example/display?image=myphoto.jpg. The server-side code might look like this: file_get_contents('/var/www/app/images/' . $_GET['image']). An attacker could change the URL to: https://target.example/display?image=../../../../etc/hostname. Because the code blindly adds the user's input to the folder path, the server attempts to read '/var/www/app/images/../../../../etc/hostname', which resolves to '/etc/hostname'. The server then displays the internal name of the computer to the attacker.
lesson.takeaway: When hunting for bugs, always look for parameters named 'file', 'path', 'doc', or 'image'. These are prime candidates for path traversal. Test by using multiple '../' sequences to ensure you reach the root directory, and try to access well-known files like /etc/passwd (Linux) or C:\Windows\win.ini (Windows). A common mistake is assuming that a '200 OK' response is enough; you must verify that the content of the response actually contains the sensitive file data you requested.
